title: Lujan v. G & G Fire Sprinklers, Inc.
lead: California directed public contractors to withhold money over disputed wage compliance, and a subcontractor challenged the absence of an administrative hearing.

actors.name: California labor officials
actors.role: Officials enforcing prevailing-wage and payroll requirements

proceedings: District court granted G & G summary judgment and enjoined enforcement.
Ninth Circuit affirmed, then reinstated its judgment after a Supreme Court remand.
limits: The Court assumed state action and a protected payment claim, and did not determine wage compliance or amounts due. Its interpretation of an alternative state contract action was tentative. Later administrative procedures were not the basis of the holding.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Wage assessments interrupt subcontract payments
sections.cue: The notices operate through awarding bodies and contractors
paragraphs: G & G Fire Sprinklers installed systems as a subcontractor on California public projects. State law required prevailing wages, payroll records, and compliance with hours provisions. Public contracts incorporated wage obligations; prime contractors were liable for unpaid wage differences and penalties, and awarding bodies withheld the assessed sums. Prime contractors could withhold corresponding amounts from their subcontractors.

In 1995 the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement found that G & G failed to pay prevailing wages and maintain or provide required payroll records on three projects. It instructed awarding bodies to withhold money from the contractors, who in turn withheld payments from G & G. The company said more than $135,000 was withheld.

The governing Code permitted a contractor or its assignee to sue the awarding body for breach of contract within ninety days after completion and acceptance. Money remained withheld during the suit, and that remedy was exclusive for contractors and their assignees. G & G objected that officials issued withholding notices without any hearing.

sections.title: The company wins a constitutional injunction
sections.cue: An earlier Supreme Court remand does not end the dispute
paragraphs: G & G sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 in the Central District of California for declaratory and injunctive relief. The district court granted summary judgment, declared the challenged provisions unconstitutional, and enjoined their enforcement against the company. A divided Ninth Circuit panel affirmed in 1998, finding a protected interest in full payment and neither a predeprivation nor postdeprivation hearing.

The Supreme Court vacated and remanded after American Manufacturers Mutual Insurance Co. v. Sullivan, which rejected state action concerning private insurers’ disputed medical payments and an entitlement before treatment was found reasonable and necessary. In 2000 the Ninth Circuit reinstated its decision. It distinguished mandatory withholding directed by state officials and emphasized that it demanded some hearing, not immediate payment while a hearing remained pending. The Supreme Court then reviewed that reinstated judgment.

sections.title: A disputed contract claim can be adjudicated in court
sections.cue: Rehnquist distinguishes present possession and occupation
paragraphs: Chief Justice Rehnquist’s unanimous opinion assumed both action under color of state law and a protected property interest in G & G’s payment claim. The question became whether ordinary state judicial process fairly protected the claim’s merits.

The Ninth Circuit had relied on cases involving seizure of a home, suspensions from occupations, and wage garnishment. Those involved present dominion over property or an existing ability to pursue an occupation. G & G instead claimed that it satisfied contractual requirements and should be paid; the State disputed compliance. A normal contract suit could fully protect that disputed entitlement. Due process did not impose an inflexible procedure across those different settings.

A prime contractor could assign its statutory action so the subcontractor could sue the awarding body. Nothing established that an assignment would be refused. G & G acknowledged earlier state suits against awarding bodies over other projects, which the Court inferred had used the assignments the Code required. Potential years of litigation created hardship, but delayed recovery was ordinary for contested contract claims and did not destroy this cause of action.

sections.title: A second possible remedy reinforces the result
sections.cue: The constitutional judgment is reversed, not the wage assessment resolved
paragraphs: Even without assignment, a contract action against the prime contractor appeared available. The exclusivity clause addressed contractors and assignees, not necessarily an unassigned subcontractor, and California’s J & K Painting decision had declined to treat failure to obtain an assignment as eliminating every remedy. The Supreme Court called its state-law conclusion tentative: California courts controlled that question and possible contractor defenses. G & G, bearing the burden of its constitutional attack, had not established that the route was closed.

On April 17, 2001, the Court reversed the Ninth Circuit. It awarded no withheld funds and decided neither compliance nor the proper amounts. California’s amended administrative scheme, effective July 1, 2001, would add an impartial hearing officer, written decision, and judicial review, but those unavailable future procedures did not support this holding. The decision rested on ordinary judicial protection of this contract claim, not a general rule that later damages always excuse a hearing.
